questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Resonance is produced between a turning fork and a resonance column tube with upper end open and lower end closed by water surface. If the frequency of the tuning fork is 800Hz, and first two resonances are observed at lengths 9.75 cm, 31.25 cm, Find the length at which the third resonance occurs? Also find the speed of sound.
questions.solution:
Let $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L_3$ be the lengths of the first, second, and third resonances respectively, and $e$ be the end correction.

The resonance lengths for a tube closed at one end are given by:
$L_1 + e = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$
$L_2 + e = \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}$
$L_3 + e = \dfrac{5\lambda}{4}$

Subtracting the first equation from the second:
$L_2 - L_1 = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

Substituting the given values:
$31.25 - 9.75 = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$
$21.50 = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 43.0\text{ cm} = 0.43\text{ m}$

The speed of sound is:
$v = f \lambda = 800 \times 0.43 = 344\text{ ms}^{-1}$

For the third resonance length:
$L_3 - L_2 = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$
$L_3 = 31.25 + 21.50 = 52.75\text{ cm}$

Answer: $52.75$ cm and $344\ ms^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The speed of transverse wave in aluminium wire is $\dfrac{1}{10}$ times the speed of longitudinal wave in the wire. The stress in the wire is (Young's Modulus of $Al = 10^{10}$ Pa)
questions.solution:
The speed of a transverse wave in a stretched wire is given by $v_t = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\rho A}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}}$, where $T$ is the tension, $\mu$ is the linear mass density, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $\rho$ is the density, and $\sigma$ is the stress in the wire.

The speed of a longitudinal wave in the wire is given by $v_l = \sqrt{\dfrac{Y}{\rho}}$, where $Y$ is the Young's modulus.

Given that $v_t = \dfrac{1}{10} v_l$, substituting the expressions yields:

$\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho}} = \dfrac{1}{10} \sqrt{\dfrac{Y}{\rho}}$

Squaring both sides gives:

$\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} = \dfrac{1}{100} \dfrac{Y}{\rho}$

$\sigma = \dfrac{Y}{100}$

Substituting $Y = 10^{10}$ Pa:

$\sigma = \dfrac{10^{10}}{100} = 10^8$ Pa.

Answer: $10^8\ Pa$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sonometer wire of length 80 cm and a tuning fork sounded together produces 5 beats per second. The same number of beats per second is produced when the length of the wire is increased to 85 cm . What is the frequency of the tuning fork?
questions.solution:
Let $f$ be the frequency of the tuning fork and $f_1, f_2$ be the frequencies of the sonometer wire at lengths $l_1 = 80$ cm and $l_2 = 85$ cm respectively. The frequency of a sonometer wire is given by $f = \dfrac{1}{2l} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, which implies $f \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$. Thus, $f_1 l_1 = f_2 l_2 = k$, where $k$ is a constant.

Given that the wire produces 5 beats per second with the tuning fork in both cases, we have $|f - f_1| = 5$ and $|f - f_2| = 5$. Since $l_2 \gt l_1$, it follows that $f_2 \lt f_1$. Therefore, $f_1 = f + 5$ and $f_2 = f - 5$.

Using the relation $f_1 l_1 = f_2 l_2$, we substitute the values:

$(f + 5) \times 80 = (f - 5) \times 85$

Dividing both sides by 5:

$(f + 5) \times 16 = (f - 5) \times 17$

$16f + 80 = 17f - 85$

$f = 80 + 85 = 165$ Hz.

Answer: 165 Hz

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An open pipe is in second harmonic with frequency $f_1$. One end of the tube is closed and frequency is increased to $f_2$ and it resonates again with nth harmonic. For what value of n , the ratio of $\dfrac{f_1}{f_2}$ is $\dfrac{4}{5}$ ?
questions.solution:
For an open pipe of length $L$, the frequency of the second harmonic is given by $f_1 = 2 \times \dfrac{v}{2L} = \dfrac{v}{L}$, where $v$ is the speed of sound.

When one end is closed, the pipe becomes a closed pipe of length $L$. The frequencies of a closed pipe are given by $f = m \dfrac{v}{4L}$, where $m$ is an odd integer ($1, 3, 5, \dots$). The $n$-th harmonic of a closed pipe corresponds to the $n$-th odd harmonic, so $f_2 = n \dfrac{v}{4L}$, where $n$ is an odd integer.

The ratio of the frequencies is given as $\dfrac{f_1}{f_2} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.

Substituting the expressions for $f_1$ and $f_2$:

$\dfrac{v/L}{n v / 4L} = \dfrac{4}{5}$

$\dfrac{4}{n} = \dfrac{4}{5}$

Therefore, $n = 5$.

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The fundamental frequency of sound produced in an open pipe of length $\mathrm{L}_1$ is same as the frequency of the $3^{\text {rd }}$ harmonic of the sound produced in the closed pipe of length $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{2}}$ Then the ratio of $\dfrac{\boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{1}}}{\boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{2}}}$ is :
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of an open pipe of length $L_1$ is given by $f_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L_1}$, where $v$ is the speed of sound.

The frequencies of a closed pipe of length $L_2$ are given by $f_n = \dfrac{nv}{4L_2}$, where $n$ is an odd integer ($n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$). The $3^{rd}$ harmonic of a closed pipe corresponds to the $3^{rd}$ overtone frequency, which is the $5^{th}$ harmonic ($n=5$). However, in many contexts, the $3^{rd}$ harmonic of a closed pipe is simply the $3^{rd}$ allowed frequency, which corresponds to $n=5$. Let us verify the standard terminology: the harmonics of a closed pipe are $1^{st}$ ($n=1$), $3^{rd}$ ($n=3$), $5^{th}$ ($n=5$). Thus, the $3^{rd}$ harmonic of the closed pipe is $f_3 = \dfrac{3v}{4L_2}$.

Equating the fundamental frequency of the open pipe to the $3^{rd}$ harmonic of the closed pipe:

$\dfrac{v}{2L_1} = \dfrac{3v}{4L_2}$

Simplifying the equation:

$\dfrac{1}{2L_1} = \dfrac{3}{4L_2}$

$\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}=\dfrac{2}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sonometer string vibrates with a frequency of 400 Hz . When the length of the string is halved and the tension is altered, it begins to vibrate with a frequency of 200 Hz . The ratio of the new tension to the original tension in the string is:
questions.solution:
The frequency of a vibrating string is given by the formula $f = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, where $L$ is the length, $T$ is the tension, and $\mu$ is the linear mass density of the string.

Let the initial frequency be $f_1 = 400$ Hz, length be $L_1 = L$, and tension be $T_1 = T$. Then $f_1 = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$.

Let the final frequency be $f_2 = 200$ Hz, length be $L_2 = L/2$, and tension be $T_2 = T'$. Then $f_2 = \dfrac{1}{2(L/2)} \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{\mu}} = \dfrac{1}{L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{\mu}}$.

Taking the ratio of the two frequencies:

$\dfrac{f_2}{f_1} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{\mu}}}{\dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}} = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{T}}$.

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{200}{400} = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{T}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2} = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{T}} \Rightarrow \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{T}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Squaring both sides:

$\dfrac{T'}{T} = \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{16}$.

Thus, the ratio of the new tension to the original tension is $1:16$.

Answer: $1: 16$

questions.q:
In a resonance column experiment, the first resonance is obtained, when the level of the water in tube is 20 cm from the open end.
Resonance will also be obtained when the water level is at a distance of

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tuning fork of unknown frequency produces 4 beats with tuning fork of frequency $310 \mathrm{~Hz}$. It gives the same number of beats on filing. The initial frequency of a tuning fork is
questions.solution:
The unknown fork produces 4 beats with 310 Hz, so its frequency is either 314 Hz or 306 Hz.

Filing increases frequency (removes mass). The beat frequency remains 4 after filing.

If initial frequency was 314 Hz: filing increases it further ⇒ difference with 310 Hz increases ⇒ beats would increase. Contradiction.

If initial frequency was 306 Hz: filing increases it toward 314 Hz ⇒ difference with 310 Hz is again 4 Hz ⇒ same number of beats. Consistent.

Initial frequency $= 306$ Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The number of possible natural oscillations of air column in a pipe closed at one end of length $85 \mathrm{~cm}$ whose frequencies lie below $1250 \mathrm{~Hz}$ are (velocity of sound $=340 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
For a pipe closed at one end, the frequencies of natural oscillations are given by the formula $f_n = \dfrac{(2n-1)v}{4L}$, where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ is the harmonic number, $v$ is the velocity of sound, and $L$ is the length of the pipe.

Given $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$ and $L = 85 \text{ cm} = 0.85 \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values into the formula:

$f_n = \dfrac{(2n-1) \times 340}{4 \times 0.85} = \dfrac{(2n-1) \times 340}{3.4} = (2n-1) \times 100 \text{ Hz}$.

We require $f_n \lt 1250 \text{ Hz}$, so:

$(2n-1) \times 100 \lt 1250$

$2n-1 \lt 12.5$

$2n \lt 13.5$

$n \lt 6.75$.

Since $n$ must be a natural number, the possible values for $n$ are $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$.

The number of possible natural oscillations is 6.

Answer: 6

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string of length $25 \mathrm{~cm}$ and mass $10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg}$ is clamped at its ends. The tension in the string is $2.5 \mathrm{~N}$. The identical wave pulses are generated at one end and at regular interval of time, $\Delta \mathrm{t}$. The minimum value of $\Delta \mathrm{t}$, so that a constructive interference takes place between successive pulses is
questions.solution:
The linear mass density $\mu$ of the string is given by $\mu = \dfrac{M}{L} = \dfrac{10^{-3} \text{ kg}}{0.25 \text{ m}} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg/m}$.

The speed of the wave $v$ in the string is $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2.5}{4 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2500}{4}} = \sqrt{625} = 25 \text{ m/s}$.

The time taken for a pulse to travel from one end to the other is $t = \dfrac{L}{v} = \dfrac{0.25 \text{ m}}{25 \text{ m/s}} = 0.01 \text{ s} = 10 \text{ ms}$.

For constructive interference between successive pulses, the pulses must return to the starting point in phase. A pulse travels to the other end (10 ms), reflects (phase change of $\pi$), and returns to the starting end (another 10 ms). The total time for a pulse to return to the start is $2t = 20 \text{ ms}$.

Since the pulse reflects at the fixed end with a phase shift of $\pi$, the next pulse must be sent such that it arrives at the start at the same time as the reflected pulse to interfere constructively. The minimum time interval $\Delta t$ is equal to the time taken for the round trip, which is $20 \text{ ms}$.

Answer: 20 ms

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With what velocity should an observer approach a stationary sound source, so that the apparent frequency of sound should appear double the actual frequency?
questions.solution:
By using $v^{\prime}=v\left[\frac{v-v_0}{v-v_s}\right]\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & 2 v=v\left[\frac{v-v_0}{v-0}\right] \\
\Rightarrow & v_0=-v
\end{array}$
Negative sign indicates that observer is moving opposite to the direction of velocity of sound.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car is moving towards a high cliff. The car driver sounds a horn of frequency $f$. The reflected sound heard by the driver has a frequency $2 f$. If $v$ be the velocity of sound, then the velocity of the car in the same velocity units, will be
questions.solution:
When the sound is reflected from the cliff, it approaches the driver of the car. Therefore, the driver acts as an observer and both the source (car) and observer are moving. Hence, apparent frequency heard by the observer (driver) is given by
where, $\quad v_s=$ velocity of sound and $\quad v_o=$ velocity of the car Thus, Eq. (i) becomes $\begin{aligned} 2 f & =f\left(\frac{v+v_o}{v-v_o}\right) \\ \Rightarrow 2 v-2 v_o & =v+v_o \Rightarrow 3 v_o=v \Rightarrow v_o=\frac{v}{3} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string vibrates with a frequency of $200 \mathrm{~Hz}$. When its length is doubled and tension is altered, it begins to vibrate with a frequency of $300 \mathrm{~Hz}$. The ratio of the new tension to the original tension is
questions.solution:
Given,
$\begin{aligned}
& v_1=200 \mathrm{~Hz}, v_2=300 \mathrm{~Hz}, \\
& l_1=l \text { and } l_2=2 l \\
& \qquad \mathrm{v}=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{v} \propto \frac{\sqrt{T}}{l} \Rightarrow \sqrt{T} \propto v \cdot l \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_2}{T_1}=\left[\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right]^2\left[\frac{l_2}{l_1}\right]^2=\left[\frac{300}{200}\right]^2\left[\frac{2 l}{l}\right]^2=\frac{9}{1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two open organ pipes A and B of length $22 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $22.5 \mathrm{~cm}$ respectively produce 2 beats per sec when sounded together. The frequency of the shorter pipe is
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe of length $L$ is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$, where $v$ is the speed of sound in air. Let $v = 330 \text{ m/s}$ be the standard speed of sound.

For pipe A with length $L_A = 22 \text{ cm} = 0.22 \text{ m}$, the frequency is $f_A = \dfrac{330}{2 \times 0.22} = \dfrac{330}{0.44} = 750 \text{ Hz}$.

For pipe B with length $L_B = 22.5 \text{ cm} = 0.225 \text{ m}$, the frequency is $f_B = \dfrac{330}{2 \times 0.225} = \dfrac{330}{0.45} = 733.33 \text{ Hz}$.

The beat frequency is $|f_A - f_B| = |750 - 733.33| = 16.67 \text{ Hz}$, which does not match the given 2 beats per second. This implies the speed of sound $v$ is not $330 \text{ m/s}$.

Let $f_A = \dfrac{v}{2 \times 0.22}$ and $f_B = \dfrac{v}{2 \times 0.225}$. The beat frequency is $f_A - f_B = \dfrac{v}{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{0.22} - \dfrac{1}{0.225} \right) = 2$.

Calculating the difference: $\dfrac{1}{0.22} - \dfrac{1}{0.225} = \dfrac{0.225 - 0.22}{0.22 \times 0.225} = \dfrac{0.005}{0.0495} = \dfrac{5}{49.5} = \dfrac{1}{9.9}$.

Substituting into the beat equation: $\dfrac{v}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{9.9} = 2 \Rightarrow v = 2 \times 2 \times 9.9 = 39.6 \text{ m/s}$.

The frequency of the shorter pipe A is $f_A = \dfrac{39.6}{0.44} = 90 \text{ Hz}$.

Answer: 90 Hz

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string vibrates with a frequency of $200 \mathrm{~Hz}$. When its length is doubled and tension is altered, it begins to vibrate with a frequency of $300 \mathrm{~Hz}$. The ratio of the new tension to the original tension is
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a vibrating string is given by $f = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, where $L$ is the length, $T$ is the tension, and $\mu$ is the linear mass density.

Let the initial frequency be $f_1 = 200 \text{ Hz}$, length be $L_1 = L$, and tension be $T_1$. Then $f_1 = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_1}{\mu}}$.

Let the new frequency be $f_2 = 300 \text{ Hz}$, new length be $L_2 = 2L$, and new tension be $T_2$. Then $f_2 = \dfrac{1}{2(2L)} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{\mu}} = \dfrac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{\mu}}$.

Taking the ratio of the two frequencies:

$\dfrac{f_2}{f_1} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{\mu}}}{\dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_1}{\mu}}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$.

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{300}{200} = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$.

Multiplying both sides by 2:

$3 = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$.

Squaring both sides:

$9 = \dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$.

Therefore, the ratio of the new tension to the original tension is $9:1$.

Answer: 9 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car is moving towards a high cliff. The car driver sounds a horn of frequency $f$. The reflected sound heard by the driver has a frequency $2 f$. If $v$ be the velocity of sound, then the velocity of the car in the same velocity units, will be
questions.solution:
Let $v_c$ be the velocity of the car and $v$ be the velocity of sound. The frequency of sound heard by the cliff (stationary observer) is $f' = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_c} \right)$.

The cliff acts as a source reflecting this frequency $f'$ back to the moving car (moving observer). The frequency $f''$ heard by the driver is $f'' = f' \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v} \right)$.

Substituting $f'$ into the equation for $f''$, we get $f'' = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_c} \right) \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v} \right) = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v - v_c} \right)$.

Given that the reflected sound heard by the driver is $2f$, we have $2f = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v - v_c} \right)$, which simplifies to $2 = \dfrac{v + v_c}{v - v_c}$.

Solving for $v_c$: $2(v - v_c) = v + v_c \Rightarrow 2v - 2v_c = v + v_c \Rightarrow v = 3v_c \Rightarrow v_c = \dfrac{v}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{v}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: With what velocity should an observer approach a stationary sound source, so that the apparent frequency of sound should appear double the actual frequency?
questions.solution:
The apparent frequency $f'$ heard by an observer moving towards a stationary source is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_o}{v} \right)$

where $f$ is the actual frequency, $v$ is the speed of sound, and $v_o$ is the velocity of the observer.

Given that the apparent frequency is double the actual frequency, we have $f' = 2f$. Substituting this into the formula:

$2f = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_o}{v} \right)$

Dividing both sides by $f$:

$2 = \dfrac{v + v_o}{v}$

$2v = v + v_o$

$v_o = v$

Answer: $v$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bat emitting an ultrasonic wave of frequency $4.5 \times 10^4 \mathrm{~Hz}$ at speed of $6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ between two parallel walls. The two frequencies heard by the bat will be
questions.solution:
The frequency of the source is $f_0 = 4.5 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$. The speed of the bat is $v_b = 6 \text{ m/s}$. The speed of sound in air is taken as $v = 330 \text{ m/s}$.

When the bat moves towards one wall, the wall acts as a stationary observer receiving the sound and then as a stationary source reflecting it back to the moving bat. The frequency $f_1$ heard by the bat from the wall it is moving towards is given by the Doppler effect formula for a moving observer and stationary source: $f_1 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v + v_b}{v} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{330 + 6}{330} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{336}{330} \right) \approx 4.58 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$.

However, considering the reflection from the wall, the frequency $f_1$ received by the bat is $f_1 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v + v_b}{v - v_b} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{330 + 6}{330 - 6} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{336}{324} \right) \approx 4.666 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz} \approx 4.67 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$.

Similarly, for the wall the bat is moving away from, the frequency $f_2$ heard by the bat is $f_2 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v - v_b}{v + v_b} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{330 - 6}{330 + 6} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{324}{336} \right) \approx 4.339 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz} \approx 4.34 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$.

Thus, the two frequencies are $4.67 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$ and $4.34 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$.

Answer: $4.67 \times 10^4 \mathrm{~Hz}, 4.34 \times 10^4 \mathrm{~Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A source of sound emits sound waves at frequency $f_0$. It is moving towards an observer with fixed speed $v_s\left(v_s \lt v\right.$, where $v$ is the speed of sound in air.) If the observers were to move towards the source with speed $v_0$, one of the following two graphs $(A$ and $B)$ will give the correct variation of the frequency $f$ heard by the observer as $v_0$ is changed.

The variation of $f$ with $v_0$ is given correctly by
questions.solution:
According to the Doppler effect, when a source of sound moving with speed $v_s$ towards a stationary observer emits sound of frequency $f_0$, and the observer moves towards the source with speed $v_0$, the observed frequency $f$ is given by the formula:

$f = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v + v_0}{v - v_s} \right)$

where $v$ is the speed of sound in air. This equation can be rewritten as:

$f = \left( \dfrac{f_0}{v - v_s} \right) v_0 + \left( \dfrac{f_0 v}{v - v_s} \right)$

This is a linear equation of the form $f = mv + c$, where $m$ is the slope and $c$ is the y-intercept. Comparing the terms, the slope $m$ is $\dfrac{f_0}{v - v_s}$ and the y-intercept $c$ is $\dfrac{f_0 v}{v - v_s}$.

Since the slope is a constant positive value, the graph of $f$ versus $v_0$ must be a straight line with a positive slope. Graph (a) represents a linear variation of $f$ with $v_0$. Therefore, graph (a) is the correct representation with a slope of $\dfrac{f_0}{v - v_s}$.

Answer: graph $A$ with slope $=\dfrac{f_0}{\left(v-v_s\right)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The string of length $2 \mathrm{~m}$ is fixed at both ends. If the string vibrates in its fourth normal mode with a frequency of $500 \mathrm{~Hz}$, then the waves would travel on it with a velocity of
questions.solution:
The frequency of the $n$-th normal mode of a string of length $L$ fixed at both ends is given by $f_n = \dfrac{n v}{2L}$, where $v$ is the wave velocity.

Given $L = 2 \text{ m}$, $n = 4$, and $f_4 = 500 \text{ Hz}$.

Substituting the values into the formula:

$500 = \dfrac{4 \times v}{2 \times 2}$

$500 = \dfrac{4v}{4}$

$v = 500 \text{ m/s}$

Answer: $500 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The displacement of a wave is given by $y=20 \cos (\omega t+4 z)$. The amplitude of the given wave is
questions.solution:
The general equation of a traveling wave is given by $y = A \cos(kx \pm \omega t + \phi)$ or $y = A \cos(\omega t \pm kz + \phi)$, where $A$ represents the amplitude of the wave.

Comparing the given equation $y = 20 \cos(\omega t + 4z)$ with the standard form $y = A \cos(\omega t + kz)$, we identify the coefficient of the cosine function as the amplitude.

Thus, the amplitude $A = 20$.

Answer: 20

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If frequencies are $(v-1)$ and $(v+2)$, then find the value of beats.
questions.solution:
The beat frequency is defined as the absolute difference between the two given frequencies.

Given frequencies are $f_1 = v - 1$ and $f_2 = v + 2$.

Beat frequency = $|f_2 - f_1|$

Beat frequency = $|(v + 2) - (v - 1)|$

Beat frequency = $|v + 2 - v + 1|$

Beat frequency = $|3| = 3$.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The equation of a progressive wave can be given by $y=15 \sin (660 \pi t-0.02 \pi x) \mathrm{cm}$. The frequency of the wave is
questions.solution:
Given, equation of progressive wave,

y=15 \sin (660 \pi t-0.02 \pi x)

Comparing this equation with standard equation of progressive wave as $y=A \sin \left(\frac{2 \pi}{T}, t-\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}, x\right)$
We get,
$\begin{aligned} \frac{2 \pi}{T} &=660 \pi \\ \Rightarrow \quad T &=\frac{2 \pi}{660 \pi} \\ \Rightarrow \quad T &=\frac{1}{330} \\ \therefore \text { Frequency of the wave, } \\ v &=\frac{1}{T} \\ &=\frac{1}{1 / 330}=330 \mathrm{~Hz} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If two waves of the same frequency and amplitude respectively on superposition produce a resultant disturbance of the same amplitude the waves differ in phase by
questions.solution:
Given that, amplitude and frequency of two waves are same.

Hence, resultant amplitude due to superposition of two waves with phase difference $\phi$ is given by

\begin{aligned}
A^{2} &=A_{1}^{2}+A_{2}^{2}+2 A_{1} A_{2} \cos \phi \\
\Rightarrow A^{2} &=A^{2}+A^{2}+2 A^{2} \cos \phi \\
\Rightarrow & A^{2}=2 A^{2}+2 A^{2} \cos \phi
\end{aligned}

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & & \cos \phi &=\frac{-1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow & & \phi &=\frac{2 \pi}{3} \end{aligned}$

Given, sound source is stationary, $v_{S}=0$
Apparent frequency, $f^{\prime}=2 f$
where, $f$ is actual frequency of sound.
By using Doppler's effect,
$\begin{aligned} f^{\prime} &=f\left(\frac{v+v_{0}}{v}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad & {[\text { where, } v \text { is velocity of sound } A .] } \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 f &=f\left(\frac{v+v_{0}}{v}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 v &=v+v_{0} \\ \Rightarrow \quad v_{0} &=v \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string vibrates with a frequency of $200 \mathrm{~Hz}$. When its length is doubled and tension is altered, it begins to vibrate with a frequency of $300 \mathrm{~Hz}$. The ratio of the new tension to the original tension is
questions.solution:
Given, $L_{2}=2 L_{1}, f_{1}=200 \mathrm{~Hz}, f_{2}=300 \mathrm{~Hz}$
We know that, frequency of vibrating string is given as

f=\frac{1}{2 L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}

where, $\mu=$ mass per unit length of string
and $L=$ length of the string.

\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & f \propto \frac{\sqrt{T}}{L} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \frac{f_{2}}{f_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}, \frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \sqrt{\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}=\frac{f_{2} L_{2}}{f_{1} L_{1}}=\frac{300}{200} \times \frac{2 L_{1}}{L_{1}} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \sqrt{\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}=3 \\
& \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}=9 \\
\therefore \quad & T_{2}: T_{1}=9: 1
\end{array}

Loudness of sound is given as

So, we get $L_{2}-L_{1}=10 \log _{10} \frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}$
here $L_{1}=30 \mathrm{~dB}, L_{2}=60 \mathrm{~dB}\begin{array}{ll}\therefore & 60-30=10 \log _{10} \frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}} \\ \Rightarrow & 3=\log _{10} \frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{I_{2}}{I_{1}}=10^{3} \Rightarrow I_{2}=1000 I_{1}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of velocity of sound in hydrogen and oxygen at STP is
questions.solution:
The velocity of sound in a gas is given by
$v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}}$
At STP, both gases are at same temperature and as they are diatomic, so their specific heat ratio $(\gamma)$ is also same. $\therefore \frac{v_{\mathrm{H}}}{v_{\mathrm{O}}}=\sqrt{\frac{M_{\mathrm{O}}}{M_{\mathrm{H}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{32}{2}}=4$ or $4: 1$

questions.q: In an experiment with sonometer a tuning fork of frequency $256 \mathrm{~Hz}$ resonates with a length of $25 \mathrm{~cm}$ and another tuning fork resonates with a length of $16 \mathrm{~cm}$. Tension of the string remaining constant the frequency of the second tuning fork is
questions.solution:
The wavelength of the sound is proportional to the length of wire. Also, the velocity of sound is same in both cases, so
$\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow & v_{1} &=v_{2} \\
\Rightarrow & & f_{1} \lambda_{1} &=f_{2} \lambda_{2} \\
\Rightarrow & 256 \times 25 &=f_{2} \times 16 \\
\Rightarrow & & f_{2}=\frac{256 \times 25}{16}=400 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The apparent frequency of a note is $200 \mathrm{~Hz}$. When a listener is moving with a velocity of $40 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ towards a stationary source. When he moves away from the same source with the same speed, the apparent frequency of the same note is $160 \mathrm{~Hz}$. The velocity of sound in air (in $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ ) is
questions.solution:
Let $f_{s}$ be the frequency of source.
The apparent frequency heard when listener moves towards source is
$f^{\prime}=f_{s}\left(\frac{v_{s}+v_{0}}{v_{s}}\right)\Rightarrow \quad 200=f_{s}\left(\frac{v_{s}+40}{v_{s}}\right)...(i)$
The apparent frequency heard, when listener moves away from source is
$\begin{aligned}
f^{\prime \prime} &=f_{s}\left(\frac{v_{s}-v_{o}}{v_{s}}\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 160 &=f_{s}\left(\frac{v_{s}-40}{v_{s}}\right)...(ii)
\end{aligned}$
Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{200}{160} &=\frac{v_{s}+40}{v_{s}-40} \\
\Rightarrow & & \frac{5}{4} &=\frac{v_{s}+40}{v_{s}-40} \\
\Rightarrow & 5 v_{s}-200 &=4 v_{s}+160 \\
\Rightarrow & v_{s} &=360 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: $90 \mathrm{~dB}$ sound is $x$ times more intense than $40 \mathrm{~dB}$ sound, then $x$ is
questions.solution:
The level of sound is given by
$L=10 \log \left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right) \mathrm{dB}$
Let for $40 \mathrm{~dB}$ sound intensity be $I$ and for $90 \mathrm{~dB}$ sound intensity be $I_{x}$, then
$40=10 \log \left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right)\Rightarrow \quad \log \left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right)=4 ...(i)$
and $\quad 90=10 \log \left(\frac{I_{x}}{I_{0}}\right)\Rightarrow \quad \log \left(\frac{I_{x}}{I_{0}}\right)=9$
Given, $\quad I_{x}=x I\Rightarrow \quad \log \left(\frac{x I}{I_{0}}\right)=9$
or $\quad \log x+\log \left(\frac{I}{I_{0}}\right)=9\Rightarrow \quad \log x+4=9 \quad$ [from Eq. (i)]
$\Rightarrow \quad \log x=5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=10^{5}$
